Adding New Functions

Use this guide when extending scalar, vector, or matrix operations. For the existing algorithms, see the Technical Guide. Choose a formulation that preserves the small quantities the result depends on, including input corrections near roots and branch boundaries.

Scalar functions

Choose the computation strategy

  1. Native double-double arithmetic. Use range reduction and a polynomial, series, or recurrence with coefficients precise enough for the error budget. Keep small offsets in their own variables when they govern relative accuracy.
  2. Compose existing functions. The inverse hyperbolic functions use tools such as log1p and sqrt. Check the accuracy of the intermediate quantities in sensitive regions.
  3. Use a guarded wider scalar function. The Double32 elementary paths use Float64 in bounded regions when converting both words preserves the exact input. Check that the result can be split back into a useful head and low word. Keep a path that retains the original representation for sensitive inputs and format limits.
  4. Convert through Float128. The gamma and error functions use this strategy. Its 113-bit significand can round away a small correction when converting a pair with widely separated components. Test the errors from input conversion, function evaluation, and conversion back to the result type.

Wire the method

  • Implementation files live under src/math/elementary/ (or src/math/special/), included from src/DoubleFloats.jl.
  • When extending a Base or SpecialFunctions operation, import it in src/DoubleFloats.jl or qualify the method definition. Export a new package-specific function if callers should be able to use it unqualified after using DoubleFloats.
  • Write for the generic signature fn(x::DoubleFloat{T}) where {T<:IEEEFloat}. Double32/Double16 variants of many functions are forwarded through Double64 by src/math/elementary/templated.jl; add your function to its list if that treatment fits.

Preserve relative accuracy at sensitive points

Identify where the function's value is small while its argument is not degenerate — that is where naïve formulas collapse:

  • Use log1p(small) to keep the small argument available to the logarithm. Forming 1 + small first can round part or all of the correction away, which matters when the result is of order small.
  • Form differences exactly. x - 1 is exact for x ∈ [0.5, 2] (Sterbenz); (1-x)/x has an exact numerator; algebraic rearrangement (1 + 2/(x-1) == (x+1)/(x-1)) can turn a cancelling formulation into an exact one. The inverse hyperbolics in archyptrig.jl are worked examples.
  • Beware inv and squaring as information destroyers: 1/x - 1 computed from inv(x) has already lost the digits that matter near x = 1; square(x) overflows for |x| > ~1e154 even when the final result is modest (asinh(2^520) is ≈ 361). Provide a large-argument branch (√(x²+1) → x for x ≥ 4/eps(T) is exact at working precision).

Bound series and choose coefficients

  • Generate coefficients at higher precision and store them as hi/lo pairs when they need double-word precision. See _expm1_coeffs in explog.jl for generated pairs. The tapered exponential kernels use scalar coefficients in higher-order terms where their contribution to the total error is small.
  • Horner evaluation can reuse the reduced argument throughout a polynomial.
  • Bound truncation over the whole reduced interval. For a series with tail term ratios bounded by r < 1, the first omitted term's magnitude divided by 1-r bounds the omitted tail. Allow margin for evaluation and reconstruction errors.
  • Series windows and branch guards must be bounded on both sides. A cautionary tale: a cos fix once guarded a small-angle Taylor kernel with x >= π/2 - π/32 — with no upper bound, everything in (π/2 + π/32, π) also fell into a kernel valid only for |r| ≤ π/32, costing 17 digits over a large interval while all existing tests passed. Write the window as lo ≤ x ≤ hi.

Handle termination and special values

  • Handle NaN, ±Inf, ±0.0 (preserve the sign of zero), and domain errors (DomainError for out-of-domain reals, matching Base), and the exact endpoints, before the general path.
  • No fixed convergence tolerances derived from inputs. An iteration's achievable floor depends on the result's scale; a tolerance computed from the initial operands can be unattainable and loop forever (agm once did). Prefer structural stopping rules: stop when the error measure stops decreasing.
  • Comparisons used to exit loops must be NaN-safe: every comparison with NaN is false, so while err > tol exits on NaN but stop when dnew >= d does not. Check isnan explicitly if an intermediate can overflow.
  • Respect representation limits honestly: if the result's lo word would be subnormal (result magnitude below ~4e-292 for Double64), full precision is impossible — do not chase it, and do not let an internal intermediate with that problem contaminate a result that is representable (rescale by exact powers of two instead; see log).

Test against a higher-precision reference

Compare with a BigFloat reference computed at 256 bits or more. For nonzero references, this snippet measures relative error in units of 2^-104. Use absolute error for an expected zero.

setprecision(BigFloat, 512)
ulps(got, want) = Float64(abs(BigFloat(got) - want) / abs(want) / big"2.0"^-104)
@test ulps(myfn(x), reffn(BigFloat(x))) < 2

Sample every region with its own tolerance:

  • random points across the whole domain;
  • dense probes at each branch boundary (both sides);
  • the sensitive points: roots, fixed points, domain endpoints — including inputs whose structure lives below one Float64 ulp, e.g. Double64(1.0, 1e-25);
  • extreme magnitudes: near floatmax, near floatmin, subnormals;
  • special values: NaN, ±Inf, ±0.0, and exact DomainError edges.

Place tests in test/ and wire the file into test/runtests.jl. The Accuracy Report describes the existing sampled checks.

Vector functions

Extend the scalar operation first. DoubleFloats.simdmap!(f, dest, x) and its two-input form already accept scalar callables, so an ordinary elementwise function needs no batch registration. Add a native kernel when a common input range admits a simpler evaluation that works across several elements at once. The User Guide describes the public calling and mutation rules.

Register a bounded kernel

Put the specialized code beside the scalar implementation. Register it with _batch_kernel, dispatching on the function, the destination element type, and the element type of each input vector. The scalar exponent accepted by ^ is passed by value, so its registration can select a kernel for one exponent. The generic registration returns nothing, which selects the scalar loop. Use the natural result type for the kernel, such as Tuple{Double64,Double64} for sincos or ComplexDF64 for cis on finite real inputs.

The reciprocal registration in src/math/ops/op_db_db.jl shows the pattern. _BatchKernel pairs an eligibility predicate with a per-element evaluator. Shared helpers and the loop are in src/math/elementary/simd.jl.

@inline _batch_inv_range(x) = _batch_abs_bounded(x, 0x1p-256, 0x1p256)

_batch_kernel(::typeof(inv), ::Type{Double64}, ::Type{Double64}) =
    _BatchKernel(_batch_inv_range, _batch_inv)

Check both components of each input. The bounded-input helpers check the high component against a chosen interval and bound the low component by half the spacing in the corresponding exponent band. Leave room for the low component at branch boundaries, and verify that intermediates stay in range and divisors stay away from zero. Reuse the scalar coefficients and error-free transforms where possible. Keep the per-element evaluator type-stable and free of allocations, side effects, exceptions, and floating-point reassociation. For native two-word Double32 arithmetic, the batch predicate can admit normalized pairs even when their sum would round in Float64. Keep the evaluator inlined so the compiler can see the arithmetic across elements.

The driver checks axes and overlap before entering the dense route. A native loop runs only after the whole block passes its predicate. A rejected block normally runs scalar calls in index order, preserving special values, destination conversion, and the writes that precede an error. The driver also handles views, overlapping storage, and custom vectors. Keep those rules in the shared driver.

Treat repair of isolated rejected elements as an optional optimization. The existing _BatchRepair handles unary Double64 inputs. It evaluates eligible lanes and safe placeholder values in one loop, then overwrites the placeholders with scalar results. Use it only where the rejected lanes admitted by the driver's wider guard can be evaluated and assigned without error. Ordinary block fallback is the starting point.

Check results and measure the whole call

This example exercises both an eligible block and scalar fallback in the same call. It compares stored components so small discrepancies and signed zeros remain visible.

using DoubleFloats

x = fill(Double64(1.125, -2.0^-58), 128)
x[end] = zero(Double64)
dest = similar(x)
reference = inv.(x)

@assert DoubleFloats.simdmap!(inv, dest, x) === dest
@assert all(isequal.(HILO.(dest), HILO.(reference)))
println("Checked reciprocal batch, including scalar fallback")
Checked reciprocal batch, including scalar fallback
  • Extend test/simd_elementary.jl. Test eligible inputs, mixed blocks, boundary points with both signs of the low component, and lengths around the 64-element minimum for the native route. Check the operation's special values, branches, output conversions, and exception order. Use the scalar result as the behavioral reference and a higher-precision calculation where the arithmetic changes.
  • Measure warmed calls with reused destinations. The benchmark driver in perf/bench_simd_elementary.jl can compare against preallocated broadcast and check allocation and mixed-input costs. Use SIMD_LLVM to dump the native loop's LLVM and check for vector arithmetic. A SIMD annotation alone cannot establish that the compiler vectorized the loop.
  • Evaluate threading separately. _batch_thread_min uses concrete argument types and defaults to no threaded execution for unlisted operations. Measure a size crossover before extending that allowlist and check the destination types admitted by _batch_thread_output. Exercise the new route with multiple Julia threads. A worker error can surface after other chunks have written.

Run the existing driver from the package root. This example compares two batch sizes with eligible inputs and with scattered exclusions.

SIMD_FILTER=inv SIMD_SIZE=4096,65536 SIMD_MIXTURE=0,0.01 \
    julia --project -t4 perf/bench_simd_elementary.jl

Record published eligibility ranges and measured crossovers in the Technical Guide.

Matrix functions

Choose the algorithm class first

  • Eigen-diagonalization (matrixfunction(fn, m)) is one line, but it fails for defective matrices and loses accuracy in proportion to cond(V) for nearly-defective ones — silently. Acceptable for functions of practically-always-diagonalizable inputs, or as a starting point clearly documented as such.
  • Dense algorithms are required for robustness:
    • series-friendly functions → scaling/squaring + Paterson–Stockmeyer (_matexp in matfun.jl is the template: scale to ‖A‖₁ ≤ 1, evaluate, square back);
    • functions with a triangular recurrence → complex Schur, operate on T, transform back (sqrt, log);
    • anything expressible through exp/log/sqrt → compose when domains and branches agree. Matrix powers use exp(p * log(A)) in the general case. The circular and hyperbolic families share polynomial and reconstruction code.

Correctness rules

  • Respect type conventions. Real input whose mathematical result is real must return a real matrix. Either stay in real arithmetic throughout (best: exp), take a hermitian shortcut when applicable, or strip imaginary roundoff dust with a tolerance guard (_strip_imag_dust) — never unconditionally real.(), which would corrupt genuinely complex results such as sqrt of a matrix with a negative eigenvalue.
  • Series bounds are norm bounds. The scalar truncation argument carries over with |x| replaced by ‖A‖; scale first so the bound is small, and remember squaring steps amplify error — keep the approximant's truncation well below 2⁻¹⁰⁴.
  • Triangular recurrences divide by Tᵢᵢ + Tⱼⱼ-type quantities; an exactly-singular case should throw (SingularException), a nearly-singular one will honestly produce large entries — match what the Float64 route does.
  • Detect hermitian input (ishermitian is exact and O(n²)) and use the symmetric path: real eigenvalues, orthonormal vectors, better speed.

Testing matrix functions

Random-matrix identity residuals alone are not enough; include:

  • defective matrices with closed forms: exp([1 1; 0 1]) = e·[1 1; 0 1], sqrt([1 1; 0 1]) = [1 ½; 0 1], nilpotent exp([0 1; 0 0]) = I + N;
  • identity residuals: sqrt(A)² ≈ A, exp(log(A)) ≈ A, sin²+cos² = I, using inputs in the functions' domains;
  • branch cases: negative real eigenvalues (complex results), exactly singular log;
  • convention checks: result eltype for real input; symmetric input giving (numerically) symmetric output — compare with a tolerance, not ishermitian, which tests exact equality;
  • Scale. A matrix with ‖A‖ ~ 100 to exercise deep scaling/squaring. Avoid identities with intrinsic cancellation amplification (exp(A)·exp(-A) = I fails at e^{‖A‖}-ish amplification for any correct implementation); compare against an eigen-reference on a symmetric matrix instead.

Wiring

Dedicated implementations go in src/math/linearalgebra/matfun.jl (or a sibling file included from matrixfunction.jl). If a function moves from the eigen route to a dedicated one, remove it from the @eval loop in matrixfunction.jl — otherwise the loop's definition silently overwrites yours (include order) or vice versa.
